records.name: Misiones
records.summary:
No Misiones-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for transgender visitors, and interior provinces without local reporting infrastructure generate few records even where risk is real — the silence reflects documentation, not demonstrated safety.

The documented picture is national and deteriorating: per a March 2026 Agencia Presentes report on the national hate-crime observatory's tally, at least 227 attacks motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity were recorded in 2025, up 62% year-on-year and the highest of the observatory's ten recorded years — one every 38 hours — predominantly by security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space, beatings the main modality, in a context the observatory attributes to the national government's 'cultural battle' against LGBTI+ people; attacks continued into early 2026, including a life-endangering home invasion of an LGBTIQ+ organisation president in another northern province. An April 2025 Washington Blade feature describes the transgender community as facing a 'chaotic, desperate situation' amid government policies; the underlying page is no longer retrievable.

records.name: Neuquén
records.summary: The national dossier found no province-specific trans statute, enforcement series or incident pattern for Neuquén; it is listed among the units classified "no sub-national signal", with the explicit caveat that most such provinces retain contravención/faltas police powers — the instrument an NGO survey holds responsible for most arrests of trans and travesti people — so "no signal" here means "no documentation", not "no exposure". The February 2025 national decrees curtailing the Gender Identity Law (minors' transition treatments; prison placement of trans detainees) apply to Neuquén as to all provinces, within a deteriorating national picture (a record 227 anti-LGBT hate crimes in 2025, up 62%).

records.name: Río Negro
records.summary: Río Negro legislated visibly on trans inclusion: a provincial statute reserves at least 1% of public-administration posts for travesti, transsexual and transgender people — one of only a handful of provinces with such a law, which signals a provincial official posture better than the national baseline, though the regional surveys found none of these quota laws was actually being complied with. In a country whose trans-death counts are small enough for one provincial case to be a real signal, the 2024 national MuMaLa registry lists a named travesti victim attributed to Río Negro (with La Pampa). As everywhere, the contravención/faltas police codes remain, and the February 2025 national decrees curtailing the Gender Identity Law (minors' transition treatments; prison placement of trans detainees) apply here too.

records.name: Santa Fe
records.summary: National sources: a record 2025 with at least 227 hate crimes on SOGI grounds (+62% year-on-year, one every 38 hours; security-force-perpetrator cases doubled, 17 to 64), the 2025 executive decrees amending the Gender Identity Law and prison housing (national, applies to every province), and trans activists' testimony on the resulting hostile climate. Against that frame this province is one of the few that measures its own exposure: the provincial government publishes violent-death statistics that include transfemicidios and travesticidios, Rosario hosts the Observatorio Mercedes Pagnutti monitoring gender violence, and national registers name Santa Fe transfemicide victims. No province-specific statute or enforcement series with a source was found.
